titel: Covid 2020 and the 2022 turn in the interest rate cycle
kurz: How the coronavirus crash became the fastest market crash in history, why the recovery came just as quickly and why, two years later, bonds offered no protection either.

bloecke.md:
On 19 February 2020, the S&P 500 closed at an all-time high. 33 calendar days later, on 23 March, it stood 33.9% lower. No bear market has ever unfolded so fast. In 1929, the first crash dragged on for weeks, and in 2008 for months.

On an intraday basis, the DAX lost just over 40% from its high on 17 February to its low on 16 March, and on a closing basis just under 39% from 19 February to 18 March. On 12 March 2020, it fell by 12.24% in a single day to 9,161.13 points. That was the second-largest daily loss in its history, surpassed only by 16 October 1989. The VIX volatility index closed at 82.69 on 16 March, the highest close in its history.

## Reasons for the rapid crash

In the second week of March, almost everything fell at the same time: shares, corporate bonds, gold and at times even long-dated US government bonds. This is the best-known case in which diversification fails, and it does not refute the principle. Investors who have to meet a margin call or pay out fund redemptions sell whatever can still be sold at all, regardless of whether they consider it overpriced. In such weeks, correlations approach one, because prices are determined by the need to pay rather than by investors' assessments.

The recovery was also unusually fast. The S&P 500 regained its previous high on 18 August 2020, 181 calendar days after the peak. The Dow Jones took until November. The DAX ended 2020 up 3.55% at 13,718.78 points. Investors who sold in March and wanted to wait until the situation calmed down bought back at higher prices than they had sold at. The situation only calmed down after prices had already recovered.

bloecke.titel: Depth and duration of market declines
bloecke.unter: Each point is a setback in the S&P 500 since 1950; depth increases to the left, and the number of months until the previous peak increases upwards. In 2020, the index fell further than in 2022 and recovered four times faster.

bloecke.md:
## How central banks and governments responded

On 15 and 16 March 2020, the Fed cut its target range to 0% to 0.25% and announced bond purchases of $700 billion. Its total assets grew from $4,174 billion at the start of 2020 to $7,335 billion at the start of 2021 and reached their peak of $8,965 billion on 13 April 2022. The Eurosystem launched the pandemic emergency purchase programme PEPP with an initial €750 billion. Its balance sheet rose from €4,664 billion at the start of 2020 to a peak of €8,836 billion on 24 June 2022. According to the US Government Accountability Office (GAO), the six US relief acts of 2020 and 2021 together provided around $4.6 trillion, of which more than $2 trillion came from the CARES Act of March 2020 alone.

In Germany, the Bundestag declared an extraordinary emergency situation in March 2020 under Article 115(2) sentence 6 GG (Basic Law) and suspended the debt brake (Schuldenbremse), and did so again in each of the two following years. Access to short-time work allowance (Kurzarbeitergeld) was made easier, and from 1 July to 31 December 2020, VAT was temporarily reduced from 19% to 16% and from 7% to 5%. After 1929, central banks and governments had tightened their policies. In 2020, what had taken months in 2008 happened within weeks. This explains the shape of the curve better than the course of the pandemic does.

## Demand shock and supply shock

Economically, 2020 was initially a demand shock. Shops were closed, trips were cancelled and the savings rate was high. The velocity of the US money supply M2 fell to 1.126 in the second quarter of 2020, the lowest value ever measured. The large amount of new money hardly circulated. German inflation was 0.5% in 2020, held down mainly by lower energy prices and the temporary VAT cut in the second half of the year. Observers who at the time inferred immediate inflation from the size of central bank balance sheets were a year too early and turned out to be right for the wrong reason.

In 2021, the picture changed. Pent-up demand met supply chains that had been geared to operating under lockdown. There were shortages of containers and semiconductors, and freight rates rose. That was a textbook [[Supply shock|supply shock]]. From February 2022, the war against Ukraine added an energy price shock. The German annual rate rose from 3.1% (2021) to 6.9% (2022). That matched 1974, and in the post-war period only 1951, at 7.6%, and 1973, at 7.1%, were higher. The monthly peak was 8.8% in October and November 2022.

bloecke.unter: The ECB only reacted when the rate was already around 7%, and then raised interest rates in larger steps than ever before in its history.

bloecke.md: The Federal Statistical Office (Destatis) regularly rebases the consumer price index to a new base year, most recently to 2020 = 100, and recalculates the series retrospectively. For December 2022, 8.6% was reported at the time, while the current series shows 8.1%. Both figures are correct; they are based on different weights in the basket of goods. When quoting historical rates, the data vintage should therefore be stated as well. Figures from newspaper archives and from today's tables come from two different indices.

## The turn in the interest rate cycle from 2022

On 27 July 2022, the ECB raised the deposit facility rate for the first time in eleven years, from minus 0.50% to 0.00%. This ended eight years of negative interest rates. Within 14 months, the deposit facility rate rose to 4.00%. In the same year, the Fed raised the upper limit of its target range from 0.25% to 4.50%, and to 5.50% by July 2023. For shares, this meant a valuation shock. The S&P 500 lost 25.4% from 3 January to 12 October 2022, and the DAX ended the year down 12.35%.

What was new, by contrast, was what happened to the bonds in portfolios.

bloecke.erklaerung: The formula gives the price of a bond without a coupon as a percentage of face value. For securities with a coupon, the coupon payments are added. In both cases, the price is the present value of all outstanding payments.
variablen: market yield for this remaining maturity, as a decimal
bloecke.beispiel: Illustrative calculation using the year-end yields on German bonds outstanding (Umlaufrendite). End of 2021, ten years, −0.28%: 100 / (0.9972)^10 = 102.84. End of 2022, nine years, 2.50%: 100 / (1.025)^9 = 80.07. Price change: 80.07 / 102.84 − 1 = −22.1%.

bloecke.md:
A ten-year German federal bond without a coupon, of the kind that existed in 2021, thus lost just over a fifth of its market value in one year. Neither a default nor a downgrade was needed for this. The loss follows solely from the arithmetic of [[Duration|duration]]. According to the rule of thumb, the price falls by roughly the duration times the change in interest rates. With a duration of around nine years and a rise in interest rates of 2.78 percentage points, the result is of the same order of magnitude.

Anyone who holds the bond until maturity still gets 100% back and thus earns the yield of minus 0.28% at which they bought it. The price loss is the result of buying at a price that only an even lower interest rate would have justified.

bloecke.unter: The annual performance of the DAX is documented, and the bond corresponds to the illustrative calculation above. The real values are the nominal ones adjusted for German annual inflation of 6.9%.

bloecke.md: In 2022, the instant-access savings account showed no loss, and yet it was one of the most expensive years of the decade. Inflation of 6.9% at 0% interest results in a [[Real return|real return]] of minus 6.5%. The German consumer price index rose from 100 (2020) to 125.8 (August 2026). Money that sat in an account over these six years has lost around a fifth of its purchasing power without a price loss ever being visible.

bloecke.md:
## Consequences for diversification

Whether bonds fall at the same time as shares depends on the type of shock rather than on a flaw in the asset class. If demand collapses, as in 2008 and in March 2020, interest rate expectations fall. Bond prices rise, and the bond portion cushions the losses. If the shock comes from the price side, interest rates rise and both halves of the portfolio lose at the same time. A portfolio of 60% shares and 40% long-dated government bonds therefore does not protect against every kind of crisis. It relies on the next shock being a growth shock. From 2000 to 2020, this calculation almost always worked out. That explains why so many investors were surprised in 2022.

There are only a few remedies against shocks from the price side, and none of them works completely. Short remaining maturities lose less in price per rate step. Inflation-linked bonds also help, although the German federal government stopped issuing new ones at the end of 2023, and the outstanding securities continue to run. In addition, there are commodities, whose prices rarely stay unchanged for long, and the willingness to sit out a real loss for a few years. None of these remedies is free. Short maturities yield less in normal times, and commodities fluctuate more than shares.

Investors who bought bonds in 2021 acquired a position that was mathematically certain to produce a real loss. For a purchase in mid-September 2026, a yield on ten-year German federal bonds of around 3.5% compared with inflation of 2.9% (August). The price loss of 2022 has thus also made the asset class capable of generating returns again. It was a one-off loss and raised the expected return on all future purchases.

Diversification across asset classes is diversification across types of shock. A portfolio that consists only of shares and long-dated bonds is broadly positioned against recessions, but not at all against inflation.

bloecke.titel: Tax consequences of the turn in the interest rate cycle
bloecke.md:
The base interest rate (Basiszins) for the [[Advance lump sum (Vorabpauschale)|advance lump sum (Vorabpauschale)]] is derived by the Bundesbank from the yield curve for federal securities (Section 18(4) InvStG (Investment Tax Act)). It was minus 0.45% in 2021 and minus 0.05% in 2022. In both years, therefore, no advance lump sum was due, regardless of how well the fund performed. For 2023 it rose to 2.55%, and for 2026 to 3.20%.

Calculation for €10,000 in an equity ETF: 10,000 × 3.20% × 0.7 = €224.00 base return (Basisertrag, Section 18(1) sentence 2 InvStG). After 30% partial exemption (Teilfreistellung, Section 20(1) InvStG), €156.80 remains. With 26.375% flat-rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer) including solidarity surcharge, this results in €41.36 of tax, which will be debited in January 2027. The advance lump sum is capped at the increase in value during the year, and tax is only due above the saver's allowance (Sparer-Pauschbetrag) of €1,000 or €2,000 (Section 20(9) EStG (Income Tax Act)).

Conversely, price losses on bonds, bond funds and mixed funds go into the general loss offset pot (Verlustverrechnungstopf) under Section 20(6) sentence 1 EStG. They can be offset against interest, dividends and fund gains. Only losses from individual shares are restricted to gains from individual shares (Section 20(6) sentence 4 EStG).

mitnehmen: At 33.9% in 33 days, the coronavirus crash was the fastest in history, and it had been recovered after 181 days because central banks and governments reacted within weeks rather than after quarters.
Depth and recovery time are barely related, because in 2022 the market fell less far than in 2020 and took four times as long to recover.
In 2022, shares and bonds fell at the same time because the shock came from the price side, and unlike in growth shocks, bonds offer no buffer against such inflation shocks.
A nominally safe account does not protect against real losses: the zero-interest account lost 6.5% in real terms in 2022, and the price level in 2026 is around a quarter above that of 2020.
The turn in the interest rate cycle also affects tax, because the base interest rate for the advance lump sum rose from minus 0.45% (2021) to 3.20% (2026).

begriffe.text: Disruption on the production side, for example through supply bottlenecks, energy shortages or a lack of workers. It raises prices and reduces output at the same time. Unlike with a demand shock, monetary policy cannot combat both at once.
Measure of a bond's sensitivity to interest rates, stated in years. According to a rule of thumb, the price changes by roughly minus duration times the change in interest rates in percentage points.

Minimum return of investment funds that is taxed in advance each year under Section 18 InvStG. It is zero if the base interest rate determined by the Bundesbank is not positive or if the fund's value has not risen during the year.
Return after deducting inflation. The correct calculation uses (1 + nominal return) divided by (1 + inflation rate), minus 1, rather than the difference between the two.
